name: Catalan (North-western)
variety: North-western Catalan (Western dialect group), described from the speech of Lleida and the surrounding plain
sources: Carbonell, Joan F. and Llisterri, Joaquim (1992). Catalan. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 22(1-2), 53-56. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.
Wheeler, Max W. (2005). The Phonology of Catalan. Oxford University Press.
Recasens, Daniel (1996). Fonètica descriptiva del català. 2nd edition. Barcelona: Institut d'Estudis Catalans.
Veny, Joan (1982). Els parlars catalans: síntesi de dialectologia. Palma: Moll.
Recasens, Daniel and Espinosa, Aina (2006). Dispersion and variability of Catalan vowels. Speech Communication 48, 645-666.
Institut d'Estudis Catalans (2016). Gramàtica de la llengua catalana. Barcelona: IEC.
Prieto, Pilar et al. (2015). Intonational phonology of Catalan and its dialectal varieties. In Frota and Prieto (eds.), Intonation in Romance. Oxford University Press.
contrasts: seven vowels under stress /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/ and five in unstressed syllables [i e a o u]; there is no schwa and no reduction of a, e to [ə] or of o to [u]
close-mid versus open-mid vowels under stress; many words with Central [ɛ] have Western [e] (cadena [kaˈðenɛ], francès [fɾanˈses], ceba [ˈseβɛ])
/s/ versus /z/ between vowels; affricates /tʃ dʒ/ where Central Catalan has initial fricatives
no /v/: written v and b are one phoneme /b/
obstruent voicing is neutralised at the end of a word
lexical stress; because unstressed vowels keep their quality, pairs such as the first and third person of verbs differ by their final vowel (canto [ˈkanto], canta [ˈkante])
allophony: unstressed vowels keep their quality; the main changes are local: initial unstressed e before s, n, m is [a] (escola [asˈkɔlɛ], entendre [anˈtendɾe], encara [aŋˈkaɾɛ])
final unstressed -a is [ɛ] in Lleida and the plain around it (casa [ˈkazɛ], porta [ˈpɔɾtɛ]); other North-western areas have [a], and the verb ending -a is widely [e]
written x and j, g are affricates at the start of a word and after a consonant: xocolata [tʃokoˈlatɛ], jove [ˈdʒoβe], gent [dʒen], menjar [menˈdʒa]; between vowels j, g are [ʒ]
the glide of the spelling ix is pronounced before the fricative: caixa [ˈkajʃɛ], peix [pejʃ]
/b d ɡ/ are approximants [β ð ɣ] after vowels and continuants; poble is [ˈpɔβle] without the gemination of Central Catalan
word-final r is silent in most words (cantar [kanˈta]) and the stop of final nt, lt, mp is silent (pont [pɔn], alt [al], camp [kam])
word-final obstruents are voiceless before pause and assimilate in voicing to a following consonant; final sibilants are voiced before a vowel
nasals assimilate in place to the following consonant
phonotactics: word-final consonant clusters are common, with the same simplifications as in Central Catalan
/ɾ/ does not begin a word; /ʎ/ and /ɲ/ occur in all positions
no word-initial /ʃ/ or /ʒ/ in the traditional dialect: they are replaced by the affricates

stress.type: lexical, on one of the last three syllables
stress.rule: Words ending in a vowel, a vowel plus s, or -en, -in are stressed on the penultimate syllable, other words on the last; all exceptions carry a written accent.
stress.cues: duration and pitch; vowel quality plays a smaller part than in Eastern Catalan because unstressed vowels are not reduced (only the contrast of open and close mid vowels is limited to stressed syllables)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none as a system: unstressed syllables have the five vowels [i e a o u]; open-mid vowels merge with close-mid ones when unstressed
rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements specific to North-western Catalan are cited here; the published Catalan figures are for other speakers.

length.notes: Geminates are rarer than in Eastern Catalan (no gemination in poble, regla); they remain in clusters such as tm, tn, tl (setmana [semˈmanɛ]).

intonation.declarative: rising accents with a delayed peak before the nucleus, low nuclear accent on the last stressed syllable and low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: both patterns of Catalan occur: a rise after a low last stressed syllable (L* HH%), and a fall on the last stressed syllable after a high stretch in questions opened by 'que'
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, falling to a low boundary
intonation.continuation: rising accent with high boundary at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: prenuclear L+<H* with the peak after the stressed syllable; nuclear L* in statements
intonation.notes: Prieto et al. (2015) cover the dialect within their survey of Catalan varieties.

problems: no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used
final unstressed a is [ɛ] in every word (the Lleida pattern), also in third person verb forms where [e] is general (dóna [dˈonɛ])
gemination is inconsistent with the dialect: regla is [rˈeɡɡlɛ] with a geminate while poble is [pˈɔβle] without
a full trill is used in every coda (porta [pˈɔrtɛ], parlar [parlˈa]) where the usual realisation is a tap
/l/ imports the English phoneme: clear before a vowel, dark only in the coda
good: no reduction to schwa and no raising of unstressed o: five unstressed vowels as in the dialect
Western close [e] in words where Central Catalan has [ɛ] (cadena [kaðˈenɛ], francès [fɾansˈes])
initial affricates (xocolata [tʃokolˈatɛ], jutge [dʒˈudʒe], gent [dʒˈen]) and the glide in caixa [kˈajʃɛ], peix [pˈejʃ]
initial unstressed e before s, n, m is [a] (estar [astˈa], entendre [antˈendɾe])
v is merged with b; final r and the stop of final nt, lt, mp are silent

notes: The voice uses rule set 2 of ca_rules (shared with Valencian) and its own phoneme table. The comment at the head of the phoneme file still says Valencian, but the content is North-western.
